concepts.name: Authorship and Dating of Natya Shastra
key_dimensions: Attribution to Bharata Muni — historical debates on single vs. multiple authorship
Estimated composition period (200 BCE – 200 CE) and textual evidence
Comparison with other foundational texts like Abhinaya Darpana and Dattilam
UPSC trap: Bharata Muni ≠ the warrior Bharata; confusion with other 'Bharata' references in literature

concepts.name: Pancham Veda — Natya Shastra as the Fifth Veda
key_dimensions: Claim that Brahma synthesized Natya Shastra from the four Vedas (words from Rigveda, music from Samaveda, gesture from Yajurveda, emotion/rasa from Atharvaveda)
Significance of labeling it 'Pancham Veda' — accessibility to all four varnas unlike the original Vedas
Philosophical distinction: Shruti (revealed) vs. Smriti (remembered) and where Natya Shastra fits
UPSC trap: Natya Shastra is NOT a Shruti text; it is a Shastra (treatise), not a Veda in the canonical sense

concepts.name: Sixty-Four Kalas (Chatushashti Kalas) — Classification of Arts
key_dimensions: Enumeration of 64 arts in Natya Shastra and Vatsyayana's Kamasutra — overlap and differences
Broad categories: performing arts, visual arts, craft arts, and knowledge arts
Distinction between Lalita Kalas (fine arts) and Upayogi Kalas (utilitarian arts)
UPSC trap: The '64 arts' appear in MULTIPLE texts (Natya Shastra, Kamasutra, Buddhist texts) with different lists — knowing which text specifies which list

concepts.name: Rasa Theory (Navarasa) — Foundation and Classification
key_dimensions: Original eight rasas in Natya Shastra vs. addition of Shanta rasa (ninth) by Abhinavagupta
Rasa-Bhava relationship: Sthayi Bhava (permanent emotion), Vyabhichari Bhava (transitory), Sattvika Bhava (involuntary)
Rasa Sutra: 'Vibhava-Anubhava-Vyabhicharibhava-Sanyogat Rasanishpattih'
UPSC trap: Shanta rasa was NOT in the original Natya Shastra — it was added later; also Karuna ≠ Shoka (the bhava)

concepts.name: Sthayi Bhavas — Permanent Emotional States
key_dimensions: Eight original Sthayi Bhavas corresponding to eight rasas (Rati→Shringar, Utsaha→Vira, Shoka→Karuna, etc.)
Distinction between Sthayi Bhava (dominant/permanent) and Sanchari/Vyabhichari Bhava (fleeting)
How Sthayi Bhavas are 'awakened' through Vibhavas (determinants) in performance
UPSC trap: Bhava is the psychological state in the performer/character; Rasa is the aesthetic experience in the audience — they are NOT interchangeable

concepts.name: Abhinaya — Four-Fold Classification of Expression
key_dimensions: Four types: Angika (bodily), Vachika (vocal), Aharya (costume/makeup), Sattvika (psychological/involuntary)
Sattvika Abhinaya as the highest form — linked to genuine emotional experience
Relationship of Abhinaya to the three performing arts: Natya, Nritya, Nritta
UPSC trap: Sattvika Abhinaya is NOT the same as Satvic guna from Samkhya philosophy, though both relate to purity/subtlety

concepts.name: Natya, Nritya, and Nritta — Tripartite Classification of Dance
key_dimensions: Nritta: Pure rhythmic movement with no expressive content (abstract/technical)
Nritya: Expressive dance combining rhythm with abhinaya (emotion and meaning)
Natya: Complete dramatic art form combining dance, music, and theatrical narrative
UPSC trap: Classical dance forms are evaluated on all three components; Bharatanatyam contains all three, but a 'Tillana' is primarily Nritta — examiners test these distinctions

concepts.name: Vrittis — Four Theatrical Styles/Modes
key_dimensions: Four Vrittis: Bharati (verbal), Sattvati (energetic/heroic), Arabhati (violent/passionate), Kaisiki (graceful/erotic)
Regional associations: Kaisiki linked to southern styles, Arabhati to northern/eastern
Dominance of Vritti in different dramatic genres (Nataka, Prakarana, etc.)
UPSC trap: Vritti ≠ Pravritti (the latter refers to regional theatrical traditions based on geography)

concepts.name: Pravrittis — Regional Theatrical Traditions
key_dimensions: Four Pravrittis: Avanti, Dakshinatya, Panchali, Odramagadhi — each linked to geographic regions
Characteristics: costume, language, music style, and movement vocabulary differ per Pravritti
Odramagadhi linked to eastern India (Odisha-Magadha region) — relevant to Odissi dance origins
UPSC trap: Pravritti ≠ Vritti; Pravritti is GEOGRAPHIC/REGIONAL style while Vritti is a MODE of theatrical expression

concepts.name: Dasharupaka — Ten Dramatic Forms Classified in Natya Shastra
key_dimensions: Ten major dramatic forms: Nataka, Prakarana, Samavakara, Ihamriga, Dima, Vyayoga, Anka, Prahasana, Bhana, Vithi
Key distinctions: Nataka (hero is noble/royal, serious theme) vs. Prakarana (hero is ordinary, invented plot)
Uparupakas — minor dramatic forms (18 in number) as a separate, often-tested category
UPSC trap: 'Nataka' as a Sanskrit dramatic form is NOT synonymous with the modern Hindi word 'Natak' (play); very specific rules govern its hero, plot, and rasas

concepts.name: Shadja-Grama and Madhyama-Grama — Ancient Scale Systems
key_dimensions: Two foundational scales (Gramas) in Natya Shastra: Shadja-Grama and Madhyama-Grama
The lost third Grama: Gandharva-Grama — mentioned but described as fallen out of use even in Bharata's time
Relationship between ancient Grama system and modern Thaat (Hindustani) / Melakarta (Carnatic) systems
UPSC trap: There are only TWO functional Gramas in Natya Shastra (not three); Gandharva-Grama is acknowledged but marked as defunct

concepts.name: Svaras — Seven Notes and Their Classification in Natya Shastra
key_dimensions: Seven svaras: Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni — their names (Shadja, Rishabha, Gandhara, Madhyama, Panchama, Dhaivata, Nishada)
Svara origins myth: each svara associated with a specific animal sound in Natya Shastra
Achala (fixed) svaras — Sa and Pa have no variants; Chala svaras have Komal/Tivra variants
UPSC trap: In Natya Shastra, the system uses 22 Shrutis (microtones) to define the svaras — the '22 shrutis' is a heavily tested concept distinct from the 7 svaras

concepts.name: Twenty-Two Shrutis — Microtonal Framework
key_dimensions: Division of the octave into 22 microtonal intervals (Shrutis) in Natya Shastra
Distribution of shrutis among the seven svaras: Sa(4), Ri(3), Ga(2), Ma(4), Pa(4), Dha(3), Ni(2) = 22
Philosophical significance: Shruti as the smallest perceptible unit of sound ('Shrutistu Akasha Sambhava')
UPSC trap: The 22 shrutis are specific to Indian classical theory and have NO direct equivalent in Western equal temperament's 12 semitones — a common comparison question

concepts.name: Murchhanas — Modal Scales Derived from Gramas
key_dimensions: Seven Murchhanas derived from each Grama by starting from successive notes (14 total: 7 from Shadja-Grama + 7 from Madhyama-Grama)
Concept of 'Amsha' (dominant note) and 'Nyasa' (final/resting note) in defining a Murchhana
Relationship of Murchhana system to later Jati system and eventually to Raga system
UPSC trap: Murchhana ≠ Raga; Murchhana is a scalar arrangement while Raga has additional grammar (ascent, descent, characteristic phrases, time theory)

concepts.name: Jatis — Melodic Entities Preceding the Raga System
key_dimensions: Eighteen Jatis described in Natya Shastra: 7 Suddha (pure) + 11 Vikrita (modified)
Ten defining characteristics (Lakshanas) of a Jati including Graha, Amsha, Nyasa, Apanyasa, Alpatva, Bahutva
Evolutionary link: Jatis → Ragas (Jatis are considered proto-ragas)
UPSC trap: The 10 Jati-Lakshanas are the PRECURSOR to Raga Lakshanas — same analytical framework, but Jati system predates the fully developed Raga system

concepts.name: Tala System in Natya Shastra — Margi vs. Desi Classification
key_dimensions: Margi Tala (universal/sacred, linked to Natya Shastra) vs. Desi Tala (regional/folk, evolved later)
Five elements of Tala in Natya Shastra: Kala, Marga, Kriya, Anga, Graha
Three speeds (Laya): Vilamba (slow), Madhya (medium), Druta (fast)

UPSC trap: 'Margi' and 'Desi' as categories apply to both Tala AND music broadly — Margi sangita is temple/classical; Desi sangita is popular/regional; this distinction is foundational to understanding the classical vs. folk divide

concepts.name: Varna — Four Types of Melodic Movement
key_dimensions: Four Varnas: Sthayi (staying on one note), Arohi (ascending), Avarohi (descending), Sanchari (wandering/mixed)
Role of Varna in defining the character and movement of a Raga
Varna in vocal music vs. Varna in dance (used to describe hand/body movement patterns in Abhinaya)
UPSC trap: 'Varna' here means melodic movement type — completely different from the social 'Varna' system; also distinct from 'Varna' (letter/syllable) in Sanskrit grammar

concepts.name: Alankara (Ornaments) — Classification in Natya Shastra
key_dimensions: 33 Alankaras described in Natya Shastra — ornamental patterns used in vocal and instrumental music
Categories: Gamaka (grace notes/oscillations) as a subset of Alankara in later texts
Comparison: Natya Shastra's Alankara system vs. later Sangita Ratnakar's expanded classification
UPSC trap: Alankara in music = melodic ornaments; Alankara in Sanskrit poetics = figures of speech (Upama, Rupaka, etc.) — two entirely different uses of the same term appearing in UPSC questions

concepts.name: Instruments Classification — Four-Fold (Chaturvidha Vadya)
key_dimensions: Four categories: Tata (chordophone/stringed), Avanaddha (membranophone/percussion), Sushira (aerophone/wind), Ghana (idiophone/solid percussion)
Examples for each: Veena (Tata), Mridangam (Avanaddha), Flute/Venu (Sushira), Cymbals/Manjira (Ghana)
Comparison with Hornbostel-Sachs Western classification system — overlaps and differences

UPSC trap: The classification is INSTRUMENT-BASED not player-based; also 'Vitata' is sometimes mentioned as a fifth category (bowed strings) in post-Natya Shastra texts — examiners test whether candidates know the original four vs. later additions

concepts.name: Sandhi and Sandhyanga — Structural Units of Drama
key_dimensions: Five Sandhis (junctions/segments of dramatic plot): Mukha, Pratimukha, Garbha, Vimarsha, Nirvahana
Sixty-four Sandhyangas — sub-elements within each Sandhi
Parallel with Aristotelian dramatic structure (Beginning-Middle-End) — a common comparative question
UPSC trap: Five Sandhis ≠ Five acts (Anka); Sandhis are PLOT STRUCTURAL divisions while Ankas are PERFORMANCE divisions — a drama can have 5-10 acts but must always have exactly 5 Sandhis
